state.thread_title: Companion planting that actually worked for me this year
state.comment: okay so I know companion planting gets memed on a lot in gardening groups as just folklore, but I want to share what actually worked in my raised beds this summer because the difference was pretty noticeable. I planted marigolds along the border of my tomato bed mostly because I had extra seedlings, and I definitely had fewer aphids on that side compared to the bed without them, though I'll admit that could just be luck or bed placement. The bigger win for me was interplanting basil between the tomato plants — not for any pest magic, but because it filled in ground space that would've otherwise gone to weeds, and it made harvesting way more efficient since I wasn't walking as far between beds. I also tried the classic beans-corn-squash combo and honestly found it kind of annoying to manage, the squash vines took over everything by August and made it hard to get to the corn. So my take is companion planting is more about smart space use and habit than any guaranteed pest control, and I'd rather hear what's actually worked for other people here than just repeat the pairing charts everyone posts. Anyone had a similarly mixed experience with the three sisters method?

state.thread_title: Why CRTs still matter for retro gaming
state.comment: CRT televisions actually have more input lag than modern LCD monitors, because the electron beam has to physically scan each line one at a time, which adds noticeable delay frame after frame. Modern LCDs process the whole image at once internally, so there's no scanning delay at all. That's why competitive retro players should really be using a modern 4K television instead of hunting down old CRTs for lower lag.

We cap screen time at forty-five minutes on weekdays and about ninety on weekends, split into two sittings rather than one block. This came after we noticed transitions off the tablet were far worse when it was one long continuous session versus two shorter ones. We also stopped counting educational apps as exempt from the total, since our son didn't distinguish between a phonics app and a cartoon in terms of the meltdown when time was up. Meals and the hour before bed are screen-free entirely, no exceptions, because we found bedtime resistance dropped noticeably once we made that consistent. I know some parents in this group have had success with token systems where kids earn extra minutes through chores or reading, and we tried a version of that for about a month, but it turned screen time into a constant negotiation rather than a settled routine, which was worse for us specifically. I don't think there's one correct number that works for every household — ours is built around our son's particular tendency to escalate at transitions, and another kid might do fine with a completely different structure. Curious whether other parents have found the two-sitting split makes a difference, or if that's just something that worked for our situation specifically.
